Confusable pairs among the rules-of-the-road distances, lane counts and yielding cases, plus continuation facts that complete part C; each block ties to one guide page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec04-R01 | anchor: A01
The same 100-foot distance marks two different no-passing zones on this page: near a bridge, viaduct or tunnel with an obstructed view, and near an intersection or railroad grade crossing. [A01]
Why it matters: group passing; confusable bridge zone versus crossing zone; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec04-R02 | anchor: A03
You should signal at least 100 feet before turning so the drivers around you can get ready. [A03]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable with the one-hundred-foot no-passing distance on the passing page; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec04-R03 | anchor: A01
On a highway outside a city, passing on the right needs pavement marked for four or more lanes, while on a city street it needs room for two or more lines of vehicles each way. [A01]
Why it matters: group passing; confusable highway versus city street; difficulty high.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec04-R04 | anchor: A02
The 500-foot figure is the distance before a stop at which a school bus starts its amber warning lights. [A02]
Why it matters: group school bus; confusable with the two-way left-turn lane limit; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec04-R05 | anchor: A05
The 500-foot figure is also the most you may travel in a center two-way left-turn lane. [A05]
Why it matters: group turn lanes; confusable with the school bus amber distance; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-R06 | anchor: A02
A moving emergency vehicle you must pull over for uses a siren or air horn with red or blue flashing lights, while the stopped-vehicle rule is triggered by red or red and blue lights on a stationary vehicle. [A02]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; confusable moving versus stationary; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec04-R07 | anchor: A02
A four-way stop goes by arrival order, an uncontrolled intersection goes to the vehicle on the right, and a roundabout goes to traffic already in the circle. [A02]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable intersection types; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0025]

FACT_ID: sec04-R08 | anchor: A03
The four-lane rule for school buses cuts both ways: drivers going the opposite way on a highway of four or more lanes need not stop, and a bus may not load or unload where riders would cross more than two lanes of such a highway. [A03]
Why it matters: group school bus; confusable driver rule versus bus driver rule; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec04-R09 | anchor: A03
The school bus suspension doubles only at a third or later offense within 5 years, to 180 days, while a second offense within 5 years stays at 90 days. [A03]
Why it matters: group school bus penalties; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec04-R10 | anchor: A01
Right-of-way rules exist for places where vehicles or pedestrians are likely to meet and no signs or signals control traffic, and they say who goes first and who waits. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; prereq for the intersection rules.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec04-R11 | anchor: A01
Intersections, vehicles inside an intersection and two-lane roads all add to the danger of passing. [A01]
Why it matters: group passing; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec04-R12 | anchor: A04
Swinging wide to the left before a right turn can lead the driver behind to think you are turning left and pass you on the right. [A04]
Why it matters: group turns; confusable right-turn versus left-turn errors.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec04-R13 | anchor: A04
On a left turn, avoid cutting the corner into traffic coming from the left, but leave room for oncoming drivers to turn left in front of you. [A04]
Why it matters: group turns; confusable with the right-turn error.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec04-R14 | anchor: A04
Turning from a two-way street onto a one-way street, start with your left wheel close to the yellow dividing line and, if the one-way road has two lanes, turn into whichever lane is free of traffic. [A04]
Why it matters: group turns; confusable with the two-way to two-way turn.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec04-R15 | anchor: A05
Roundabouts lower fatal and injury crashes by cutting speeds and removing left turns across opposing traffic, and every entering leg has a yield sign. [A05]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec04-R16 | anchor: A06
If you miss your exit in a roundabout, keep circling until you reach it, and give trucks and trailers room because they may use more than one lane. [A06]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; continuation of roundabout conduct.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-R17 | anchor: A06
A truck apron is the paved inner area of a roundabout for the rear wheels of large trucks, and cars, SUVs and pickup trucks must not use it. [A06]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; glossary truck apron.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-R18 | anchor: A06
At a J-turn intersection on a four-lane highway, instead of crossing fast traffic you turn right with traffic, merge to the far left lane, and then turn left in the direction you want to go. [A06]
Why it matters: group intersections; glossary J-turn.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec04-R19 | anchor: A06
Cities, counties and the state can all set traffic rules, and you must obey each; local rules may set speed limits, one-way streets and stop signs, keep commercial vehicles off certain streets, control parking and turns, require signals, brake lights and horns, or ban sound-producing warning devices. [A06]
Why it matters: group local ordinances; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0029]
